metadata.name: Rural CHW screening rule set (UNAPPROVED TEMPLATE)
metadata.disclaimer: THIS FILE IS A CONFIGURATION TEMPLATE, NOT AN APPROVED CLINICAL PROTOCOL. The thresholds below are placeholders drawn from widely published general-reference danger-sign values so that the engine can be exercised end to end. They have NOT been reviewed or approved by any clinical authority. Before any use involving real patients, the responsible health authority must review every rule, replace the thresholds with those of the locally approved protocol, record the approver in metadata.approvedBy and the approval date in metadata.approvedOn, and raise rulesetVersion. The application is a decision-support tool for trained Community Health Workers and never replaces the judgement of a qualified clinician.
metadata.source: Placeholder values pending local clinical protocol approval.

defaultResult.recommendation: No danger signs were detected in this screening. Share the relevant health awareness message, advise the patient to return if they feel worse, and continue routine monitoring at the next scheduled visit.

rules.name: Signs of circulatory shock
rules.label: Low blood pressure with a very fast pulse
rules.recommendation: This is an emergency. Refer the patient to the nearest facility immediately and arrange transport now. Keep the patient lying down and warm while you wait.
rules.explanation: Low blood pressure together with a racing pulse is a recognised emergency pattern that needs facility care without delay.

rules.name: Danger sign in a child under five
rules.label: Danger sign in a child under five
rules.recommendation: This is an emergency. Refer the child to the health facility immediately and arrange transport now.
rules.explanation: These are danger signs in the WHO/UNICEF chart for caring for the sick child in the community. A child with any of them is referred urgently.

rules.name: Fever with convulsions or confusion
rules.label: Fever together with convulsions, confusion or reduced consciousness
rules.recommendation: This is an emergency. Refer immediately and arrange transport now. Do not leave the patient alone.
rules.explanation: Fever combined with any change in consciousness is among the most urgent danger signs in the protocol.

rules.name: Low oxygen saturation
rules.label: Low oxygen level in the blood
rules.recommendation: Refer the patient to the health facility immediately. Arrange transport now.
rules.explanation: An oxygen reading below this level is an urgent danger sign in every protocol this system supports.

rules.name: Very low blood glucose
rules.label: Very low blood sugar
rules.recommendation: If the patient is awake and able to swallow, give sugar or a sweet drink now, then refer immediately.
rules.explanation: Low blood sugar can deteriorate quickly and is treated before and during referral.

rules.name: Positive malaria test with a danger sign
rules.label: Positive malaria test with a danger sign
rules.recommendation: Severe malaria is possible. Refer to the health facility immediately with a referral letter. If you are trained in community case management, give the pre-referral treatment from your kit before the patient leaves.
rules.explanation: Malaria with fits, confusion, inability to feed or vomiting everything can kill within hours and needs facility treatment.

rules.name: General danger sign
rules.label: Danger sign: fits, not fully awake, confused, cannot eat or drink, vomits everything, or chest pulling in
rules.recommendation: This is an emergency. Refer to the health facility immediately and arrange transport now. Do not leave the patient alone.
rules.explanation: Each of these signs is urgent by itself, with or without a fever or a positive malaria test.

rules.name: Danger sign during pregnancy (WHO)
rules.label: Danger sign during pregnancy
rules.recommendation: This is an emergency. Refer to the hospital or health centre immediately, day or night, without waiting, and arrange transport now. Give her a referral letter.
rules.explanation: WHO PCPNC (C15) lists this among the signs for which a pregnant woman should go to the hospital or health centre immediately, day or night, without waiting: vaginal bleeding, convulsions, severe abdominal pain, fast or difficult breathing. Reduced fetal movement is also included.

rules.name: Raised blood pressure with persistent headache
rules.label: Very high blood pressure together with a persistent headache
rules.recommendation: Refer the patient to the health facility immediately. Do not wait for the next visit. Arrange transport if you can, and record the referral before you leave.
rules.explanation: A blood pressure this high combined with a headache that has lasted several days is one of the danger-sign patterns the protocol asks you to escalate the same day.

rules.name: MUAC in the red band
rules.label: MUAC tape reads red (severe malnutrition)
rules.recommendation: Refer to the health facility today for treatment of severe acute malnutrition. Give the caregiver a referral letter and agree when you will visit again.
rules.explanation: A red MUAC reading marks severe acute malnutrition, which carries a high risk of death without treatment.

rules.name: Swelling of both feet in a child
rules.label: Swelling of both feet in a child under five
rules.recommendation: Refer to the health facility today. Swelling of both feet in a young child is a sign of severe malnutrition.
rules.explanation: Bilateral pitting oedema is a sign of severe acute malnutrition whatever the MUAC reading.

rules.name: Severe headache or blurred vision in pregnancy (WHO)
rules.label: Severe headache or blurred vision during pregnancy
rules.recommendation: Refer to the hospital or health centre immediately, day or night, without waiting. These can be signs of pre-eclampsia, which can lead to fits.
rules.explanation: WHO PCPNC (C15) lists this among the signs for which a pregnant woman should go immediately ("severe headaches with blurred vision"); WHO also treats severe headache and blurred vision as priority signs of pre-eclampsia.

rules.name: Fever and too weak to get out of bed (WHO)
rules.label: Fever and too weak to get out of bed during pregnancy
rules.recommendation: This is an emergency. Refer to the hospital or health centre immediately, day or night, without waiting, and arrange transport now.
rules.explanation: WHO PCPNC (C15) lists this among the signs for which a pregnant woman should go immediately ("fever and too weak to get out of bed"); it can mean a severe infection such as malaria or sepsis.

rules.name: Vomiting everything together with diarrhoea
rules.label: Losing fluid from both vomiting and diarrhoea
rules.recommendation: Refer to the health facility immediately. Give oral rehydration solution in small sips on the way if the patient can swallow at all, and tell the facility that both signs are present.
rules.explanation: Losing fluid two ways at once dehydrates a patient far faster than either sign alone, and the very young and the very old can deteriorate within hours.

rules.name: Raised blood pressure in pregnancy
rules.label: Raised blood pressure during pregnancy
rules.recommendation: Refer to the health facility today for assessment. Do not wait for the next antenatal visit.
rules.explanation: The blood pressure threshold that triggers referral in pregnancy is lower than for other adults.

rules.name: Fast breathing in an infant under one year
rules.label: Breathing is too fast for a baby of this age
rules.recommendation: Refer to the health facility immediately. Carry the baby upright, keep them warm, and do not delay to finish the rest of the screening.
rules.explanation: Breathing rate is counted against the age of the child, because what is normal for an adult is dangerously fast for an infant. A rate this high in a baby under one is a referral sign on its own.

rules.name: Fast breathing in a child aged one to four
rules.label: Breathing is too fast for a child of this age
rules.recommendation: Refer to the health facility immediately. Keep the child calm and upright, and record the breathing count you took so the facility does not have to start again.
rules.explanation: The threshold is lower than for a baby and higher than for an adult, because normal breathing rate falls as a child grows.

rules.name: Difficulty breathing
rules.label: Difficulty breathing
rules.recommendation: Refer the patient to the health facility immediately. Keep them sitting upright and calm.
rules.explanation: Breathing difficulty is a danger sign that is escalated the same day.

rules.name: Long illness in a child under five
rules.label: Cough or diarrhoea for 14 days or more, or fever for 7 days or more
rules.recommendation: Refer the child to the health facility urgently and give the caregiver a referral letter. If the child can drink, give fluids and continue feeding on the way.
rules.explanation: The WHO/UNICEF chart for caring for the sick child in the community treats an illness lasting this long as a danger sign that needs the health facility.

rules.name: Fever in an infant under one year
rules.label: A baby under one year has a fever
rules.recommendation: Refer to the health facility immediately, even if the baby seems otherwise well. Do not give anything other than breast milk or oral rehydration solution on the way.
rules.explanation: Infants can be seriously unwell with very few other signs, so fever at this age is escalated rather than watched.

rules.name: Severely raised blood pressure
rules.label: Severely raised blood pressure
rules.recommendation: Refer the patient to the health facility today. Record the reading on the referral note so the facility can see it.
rules.explanation: Readings at this level are treated as urgent regardless of whether the patient currently feels unwell.

rules.name: Very high fever
rules.label: Very high temperature
rules.recommendation: Refer the patient to the health facility today. Encourage fluids and keep them cool while arranging transport.
rules.explanation: A temperature at this level needs assessment and testing that a CHW cannot provide in the village.

rules.name: Very high blood glucose
rules.label: Very high blood sugar
rules.recommendation: Refer the patient to the health facility today. Encourage the patient to drink water while transport is arranged.
rules.explanation: A reading this high needs facility assessment on the same day.

rules.name: Weight loss with a persistent cough
rules.label: Losing weight alongside a cough that will not clear
rules.recommendation: Refer to the facility for assessment and testing. Explain that the test is straightforward and that going early makes treatment easier, because this is a pattern people often delay acting on.
rules.explanation: This combination is one the protocol asks to have investigated rather than watched. The CHW is not diagnosing anything here — they are getting the patient to the test.

rules.name: Fever during pregnancy (WHO)
rules.label: Fever during pregnancy
rules.recommendation: She should go to the health centre as soon as possible, today or tomorrow. Advise her to keep drinking fluids, and to go immediately if she becomes too weak to get out of bed.
rules.explanation: WHO PCPNC (C15) lists this among the signs for which a pregnant woman should go to the health centre as soon as possible. Fever with weakness is an immediate danger sign (MAT-RED-04).

rules.name: Go to the health centre soon (WHO)
rules.label: Abdominal pain, feeling ill or swelling during pregnancy
rules.recommendation: She should go to the health centre as soon as possible, today or tomorrow, to be checked. Go immediately if the pain becomes severe, she bleeds, has a fit, or gets a severe headache with blurred vision.
rules.explanation: WHO PCPNC (C15) lists this among the signs for which a pregnant woman should go to the health centre as soon as possible: abdominal pain, feels ill, swelling of fingers, face or legs.

rules.name: Persistent vomiting in pregnancy
rules.label: Cannot keep food or fluids down while pregnant
rules.recommendation: Refer to the facility within 24 hours. Encourage small, frequent sips of clean water or oral rehydration solution in the meantime, and ask a family member to watch for drowsiness.
rules.explanation: A mother who cannot keep fluids down can become dehydrated quickly, and dehydration in pregnancy affects both her and the baby.

rules.name: Diarrhoea with severe stomach pain in a child
rules.label: Diarrhoea together with severe stomach pain
rules.recommendation: Refer to the facility within 24 hours. Start oral rehydration solution now and show the carer how to continue it, and explain that the child must be brought straight in if they stop drinking or become drowsy.
rules.explanation: Diarrhoea alone is common, but with severe pain it needs assessment sooner than the next routine visit.

rules.name: Possible tuberculosis
rules.label: Cough with night sweats or weight loss (possible TB)
rules.recommendation: Refer to the health facility for a TB test (sputum). Advise the patient to cover their mouth when coughing and to keep rooms ventilated until they are tested.
rules.explanation: Cough with night sweats or weight loss is a common screening sign for tuberculosis and should be tested at a facility.

rules.name: Prolonged diarrhoea in a child
rules.label: Diarrhoea lasting three days or more in a young child
rules.recommendation: Give oral rehydration advice today and arrange follow-up within two days. Refer if the child cannot drink or becomes drowsy.
rules.explanation: Diarrhoea that lasts several days risks dehydration and needs close follow-up.

rules.name: Positive malaria test
rules.label: Positive malaria test
rules.recommendation: If you are trained in community case management and the patient has no danger signs, treat with the malaria medicine in your kit as the national guidelines describe; otherwise refer to the health facility. Visit again in three days, and refer at once if the patient gets worse.
rules.explanation: Uncomplicated malaria can be treated in the community by a trained VHT, but must be followed up.

rules.name: Blood in stool in an older child or adult
rules.label: Blood in stool
rules.recommendation: Refer to the health facility within 24 hours to find the cause. Give oral rehydration solution if there is also diarrhoea, and go immediately if the patient becomes weak or cannot drink.
rules.explanation: Blood in stool needs a cause found at a facility. In a child under five it is a danger sign and is handled by a separate rule.

rules.name: Persistent cough
rules.label: Cough lasting two weeks or more
rules.recommendation: Refer the patient to the health facility for screening within one week.
rules.explanation: A cough lasting two weeks or more is the standard trigger for facility screening.

rules.name: Fever pattern suggesting malaria in an endemic area
rules.label: Fever with chills or body aches
rules.recommendation: Refer the patient for a malaria test at the health facility within 24 hours. Share the malaria awareness message today.
rules.explanation: In a malaria-endemic area this pattern is the trigger for a diagnostic test; the CHW does not diagnose malaria in the village.

rules.name: Very low blood pressure
rules.label: Unusually low blood pressure
rules.recommendation: Check the patient is not dizzy or dehydrated, offer fluids, and repeat the measurement. Arrange follow-up within one week.
rules.explanation: A low reading can indicate dehydration or blood loss and should be rechecked rather than ignored.

rules.name: Raised blood pressure without danger signs
rules.label: Raised blood pressure
rules.recommendation: Arrange a follow-up visit within two weeks and repeat the blood pressure measurement. Share the hypertension awareness message with the patient today.
rules.explanation: A single raised reading is not a diagnosis. The protocol asks for a repeat measurement before the patient is referred for assessment.

rules.name: MUAC in the yellow band
rules.label: MUAC tape reads yellow (moderate malnutrition)
rules.recommendation: Counsel the caregiver on feeding, link the family to the nutrition programme at the health facility, and measure the arm again in two weeks.
rules.explanation: A yellow MUAC reading marks moderate acute malnutrition, which can become severe without support.

rules.name: Prolonged diarrhoea in an older child or adult
rules.label: Diarrhoea that has lasted several days
rules.recommendation: Arrange a follow-up within the week and start oral rehydration solution now. Advise the patient to go to the facility straight away if they cannot keep fluids down, pass blood, or become drowsy.
rules.explanation: Diarrhoea lasting several days needs a cause found, and the patient needs rehydrating while that happens.

rules.name: Fever
rules.label: Raised temperature
rules.recommendation: Advise fluids and rest, and arrange a follow-up within two days. Refer if the fever does not settle or the patient becomes worse.
rules.explanation: A moderate fever is monitored first; it is escalated if it persists or if danger signs appear.

rules.name: Raised blood glucose
rules.label: Raised blood sugar
rules.recommendation: Refer the patient for a confirmatory test at the facility within one week. Share the diabetes awareness message today.
rules.explanation: A single raised reading is not a diagnosis; the facility confirms it before treatment begins.

rules.name: Abnormal pulse rate
rules.label: Pulse outside the expected range
rules.recommendation: Rest the patient for five minutes and measure again. If it remains outside the normal range, arrange follow-up within one week.
rules.explanation: A single abnormal pulse is often temporary; the protocol asks for a repeat measurement at rest.

rules.name: Raised respiratory rate
rules.label: Faster breathing than expected
rules.recommendation: Arrange a follow-up within three days and recheck the breathing rate. Refer sooner if the patient becomes short of breath.
rules.explanation: In a patient aged five or over, a raised breathing rate can be the first sign of a chest infection and is worth rechecking. Children under five are assessed against their own age thresholds.

rules.name: Possible undernutrition in a child
rules.label: Reported weight loss in a young child
rules.recommendation: Refer the child to the facility for nutritional assessment within one week and share the nutrition awareness message.
rules.explanation: Weight loss in a young child is assessed at the facility, where growth can be plotted properly.

rules.name: Older adult with dizziness and fatigue
rules.label: An older patient is dizzy and very tired
rules.recommendation: Arrange a follow-up within the week and check the blood pressure sitting and then standing if you are able. Ask whether they have fallen recently, and advise them to stand up slowly.
rules.explanation: These two signs together in an older person are worth a proper look, most often because of the risk of a fall rather than because of any one illness.

rules.name: Severe symptom reported
rules.label: A symptom the patient describes as severe
rules.recommendation: Arrange a follow-up within two days. Refer sooner if the symptom worsens or new danger signs appear.
rules.explanation: A symptom the patient rates as severe is followed up even when the measurements look normal.

rules.name: Antenatal care reminder
rules.label: Pregnant: antenatal care and birth plan (WHO)
rules.recommendation: No danger signs today. WHO recommends at least eight antenatal care contacts: encourage her to attend the next one and to give birth at a health facility. Help her make a birth and emergency plan (where she will go, how she will get there, saving for the costs, who will go with her), tell her the danger signs that mean going immediately, and agree when you will visit again.
rules.explanation: WHO (2016) recommends a minimum of eight antenatal care contacts, and PCPNC (C14–C15) asks every pregnant woman to have a birth and emergency plan and to know the danger signs.
